summary: Redwood AE+SE walked Atlas Health through the Console tracing UI, error analysis flows, and request logs search. Customer cares about deterministic latency, data residency, and root-cause debugging for production errors. Agreed next steps: share security docs, exchange sample logs, and kick off a short POC on dedicated capacity to reproduce their error patterns.
topics: Debugging flows and correlating traces to requests
transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/time: 2027-01-15 16:00 UTC
- Duration: ~48 minutes
- Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Lena (Atlas Head of ML), Raj (Infra), Samir (CTO)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you making time. Quick intros - I'll be Maya, AE at Redwood, and Diego's our solutions engineer, he'll do most of the live walkthrough.
[00:15] Lena: Hi, Lena here. Quick context - we're running inference for a patient-facing assistant, multi-tenant, and we've been seeing intermittent 5-10x latency spikes and a handful of errors during peak.
[00:30] Raj: Yeah, hi, Raj. We're on GCP, using internal autoscaling and a mix of on-demand GPUs. Primary concerns are PII and HIPAA controls, also we want predictable tail latency.
[00:45] Diego: Great, that's perfect context. Today I'll show the Console tracing UI, how error analysis ties into request logs, and the debugging flow you can use to find root cause - and we'll point out where Dedicated or Private options help.
[01:10] Maya: Quick agenda - tracing overview, demo: follow a failing request from trace to logs, error analysis workspace, then POC next steps. Sound good?
[01:22] Samir: Yep, go ahead.

[02:00] Diego: Ok switching to the Console - first, Trace explorer. The UI collects span-level traces for each request, we show latency distribution, and you can filter by model, route, region, and a custom tag, e.g., customer_id.
[02:30] Diego: Notice the microburst on that timeline - you can zoom in to see individual traces and click into a trace detail. Each span includes host, kernel version, and if available, the KV cache hit/miss markers.
[03:05] Lena: KV cache markers? sometimes our logs show "K V cache cold" but not correlated to traces.
[03:20] Diego: Yeah transcription sometimes shows K V, we surface a "kv_cache_hit" tag when the runtime responds without loading weights from disk. You can filter traces where kv_cache_hit=false.
[03:40] Raj: That would help - our infra team suspects cache thrash when multiple versions roll out.

[04:15] Diego: Now the trace detail pane - here's an example of a slow request. Top-level span shows total token time, inner spans show model forward, kernel compile if any, network hop to external vector store, and post-processing. You can expand to see stderr snippets captured by the runtime.
[04:45] Diego: Notice here a kernel fallback happened - the runtime logged a compile and then a slower path. We tag those so you can search across traces for "kernel_compile" events.
[05:10] Lena: That's super useful. Can we export traces for offline analysis?
[05:20] Diego: Yes, export to JSON or link a trace to S3. We can also integrate with your internal tracing system via the webhook.

[06:00] Maya: Quick note - on Dedicated you get longer retention and more verbose traces by default, which helps for long tail debugging.
[06:20] Samir: What about PII - are traces stripped or encrypted?
[06:30] Diego: Good question. Traces can be redacted at capture time with rule-based scrubbing. We also support customer-managed keys for storage encryption and we can disable payload capture in Private mode.

[07:15] Diego: Now moving to Error Analysis workspace - this aggregates failed responses by error type, model, and route. You can create a cohort of failing prompts and run automated regression checks.
[07:40] Diego: For example, here we group by "generation_timeout" and "nucleus_sampling_error" - clicking into a cohort shows representative requests, stack traces, and frequency over time.
[08:05] Raj: Is the "generation_timeout" from Redwood runtime or from our wrapper?
[08:10] Diego: It's minted by the runtime when token generation exceeds configured SLO; we also forward upstream timeouts from downstream calls if they exist. So you get both sources.

[09:00] Diego: Linking traces and request logs - in the Request Logs tab you can search by request_id, user_id, or text regex. Results show duration, model, route, and a link to the full trace.
[09:30] Lena: Can we bulk query by a list of request IDs? Our support ticket numbers are mapped to request IDs.
[09:40] Diego: Yes we have a bulk upload field; you can paste a CSV of ids and the UI will batch fetch traces and show a consolidated heatmap.

[10:10] Diego: Demoing a failing flow now - here's a real example (anonymized). We'll filter for route "patient-summaries" and error "out_of_memory". You can see a cluster of failures at 14:32 UTC.
[10:35] Diego: Click into one trace - inner spans show GPU memory spike during model load, then a fallback to CPU path which caused a 6x latency increase.
[10:50] Raj: That matches the time we rolled a new quantized model. Could be memory accounting change.

[11:20] Diego: From this view you can create an "Investigate" ticket that includes trace links, stack snippets, and logs. It also suggests mitigation: pin previous model version, enable pre-warming cache, or increase reserved memory on Dedicated.
[11:45] Lena: Can the system automatically alert on these clusters?
[11:50] Diego: Yes - you can create alerts based on error rate thresholds, or cluster detection for specific error signatures. Alerts integrate with PagerDuty/Slack.

[12:30] Maya: Quick pause - can I ask about data residency? We have a Canadian region requirement for PHI.
[12:40] Diego: We support region pinning; you can route requests to a specific region and we can guarantee storage in-region on Private/Dedicated. Hosted has region coverage but for strict compliance customers we recommend Private deployment.

[13:15] Samir: If we go Dedicated, can we run the tracing plane on our VPC?
[13:25] Maya: With Redwood Private you can run the control plane in your VPC or on-prem; traces can be stored in your S3 with customer-managed keys.

[14:00] Diego: Back to errors - here's the request logs search. You can filter by response code, token count, latency buckets, and include a regex on the prompt. There's an ability to correlate with model version metadata (quantization, kernels).
[14:30] Diego: See this example where prompt length spikes correlate with a specific downstream vector DB call.

[15:05] Lena: Are the request logs immutable and tamper-evident? We need auditability.
[15:15] Diego: We provide append-only logs with integrity checks and support audit exports. In Private mode you can use your own logging pipeline and HSM-backed keys.

[16:00] Diego: Now quick walkthrough of debugging flow - step 1: isolate failing cohort in Error Analysis; step 2: find representative traces; step 3: check kernel/compiler events and kv_cache hits; step 4: correlate with infra metrics and request logs; step 5: apply mitigations or rollback model.
[16:35] Raj: How does automated batching affect tail latency visibility?
[16:45] Diego: Batching can inflate apparent per-request latency in traces because of queueing; we tag batch boundaries and provide per-token breakdown so you can separate queue wait vs execution time.

[17:20] Diego: Also, we surfaced a delta view: before/after a rollout you can compare trace distributions and run an A/B analyze in the Console. Very helpful for quantization rollouts.
[17:45] Lena: Nice. Can we get those delta reports programmatically?
[17:50] Diego: Yes, there's an API endpoint and you can schedule daily report exports.

[18:30] Maya: Quick commercial note - Dedicated gives you SLA for throughput and lower variance; there's also a burst tier for peak activity.
[18:45] Samir: Pricing ballpark?
[18:50] Maya: I'll send the dedicated commitment tiers, and we can tailor based on the POC results.

[19:20] Diego: Back to a specific debugging example - here's a multi-span trace where the network hop to your external vector DB timed out intermittently; the runtime logged both a retry and a fallback. You can instrument the DB call with a custom span to see the timings end-to-end.
[19:50] Raj: Our vector DB is internal, we can add spans but we'd prefer Redwood to correlate automatically.
[20:00] Diego: We have an SDK to automatically instrument downstream calls and inject correlation IDs. That way traces show the DB call timing inline.

[21:10] Lena: A couple of operational questions: retention length for traces and logs, and cost of verbose capture?
[21:20] Diego: Hosted default retention is 30 days for traces and 90 days for request logs. Dedicated can extend to 365+ with tiered storage. Verbose capture increases storage; we provide sampling and rule-based capture to limit costs.

[22:00] Samir: Any known gotchas with GPU pooling and warm starts?
[22:10] Diego: Warm starts rely on KV cache persistence and model layout. If you frequently change model variants it can cause cache churn - we recommend pinning model shards in Dedicated for high QPS.

[23:00] Diego: Now I'll show a quick workflow to create a canary rollout: define two model variants, route 5% traffic to new one, enable delta trace comparison and auto-fallback on error rate > 2%.
[23:30] Diego: The Console shows a side-by-side with example traces for each variant, and the error analysis will surface regressions per prompt set.

[24:10] Lena: For our HIPAA posture, will the canary traffic contain PHI?
[24:20] Diego: You control that - you can scrub PII in transit or route canary to a private environment with no payload capture. We also offer synthetic prompt sets for regression tests.

[25:00] Raj: About request logs format - JSON lines? Parquet?
[25:05] Diego: We export as JSONL and can push to Parquet in your S3 for long-term analytics.

[26:00] Diego: Demoing search now - here's a regex search that surfaces 37 matches for a failing tokenization edge case. You can save searches as saved views for your ops playbooks.
[26:30] Lena: Can saved views be scoped by org/team RBAC?
[26:35] Diego: Yes, RBAC scopes saved views and dashboards; we integrate with SSO/SAML and OIDC groups.

[27:10] Maya: Quick question - who will be the internal champion for the POC?
[27:20] Lena: That'll be me for ML, Raj will handle infra, and Samir will sponsor at exec level.

[28:00] Diego: Last part - integration points: trace webhooks, S3 export, alerting to Slack/PagerDuty, and API access for scripted delta reports.
[28:20] Diego: Also note we have an Optimize module that will recommend quantization and batching profiles based on your historical traces. It can suggest lower-cost model variants with similar quality.

[29:10] Lena: How trustworthy are the Optimize recommendations? Do they run evals?
[29:15] Diego: They run dataset-driven evals against your prompt set (if shared) and provide quality/regression metrics along with cost deltas.

[30:00] Samir: OK, can we align on next steps?
[30:05] Maya: Yes - we'll send security docs and pricing, Diego will share a POC checklist and a test harness, and Lena will share sample failing request IDs.

[30:20] Raj: For the POC, we'd want a 3-day stress run and a 1-week tail-latency run.

[31:00] Diego: That's doable. We'll propose a POC plan that includes synthetic traffic to reproduce memory and cache scenarios plus a live replay of your sample logs.

[32:10] Lena: One last technical - can you show how to link a trace back to a support ticket in the UI?
[32:20] Diego: Sure - in trace detail there's a "Create Investigate" button. You can paste the ticket ID or it will auto-populate if your ticketing system is integrated. Here's a demo create - it bundles trace URL, logs snippet, and suggested mitigations.

[33:15] Maya: Anything else from Atlas?
[33:20] Samir: No, looks good. We want to review the SOC docs before POC sign-off.

[34:00] Diego: Quick recap of the debugging flow and the primary mitigation levers - pin model version, pre-warm KV cache, adjust batching settings, or increase reserved memory on Dedicated.

[34:30] Lena: On the pre-warm, is that a manual process or can Redwood auto-warm on deploy?
[34:40] Diego: You can configure auto-warm on rollout; we also have an API to programmatically warm specific prompts.

[35:10] Maya: I'll follow up with an email summarizing the POC scope and attach the security pack.

[36:00] Samir: Good, we'll look at dates - target late Jan for POC start.

[37:00] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll action the items.

[38:00] Diego: One tiny demo add-on - request logs supports fuzzy text matching for prompts which helped a customer find malformed Unicode inputs that caused tokenization errors.

[39:10] Raj: For the POC infra, will we need to open ports to Redwood?

[39:20] Maya: We'll share a networking diagram; for Dedicated there's an option to peering or private link, for Private you can keep egress blocked and run the control plane inside your VPC.

[40:00] Diego: Final note - we capture lightweight environment metadata in traces: CUDA driver version, kernel name, model hash. When customers report regressions we often identify a mismatched driver or quantization difference.

[41:00] Lena: Perfect. We'll aim to send the sample logs by the 20th.

[41:30] Maya: Great, appreciate it. We'll send the docs and proposed POC plan.

[42:00] Samir: Thanks, talk soon.

[42:10] Maya: Bye all.

[43:00] -- meeting ends --

Notes about transcription: occasional ASR errors (e.g., "K V cache" instead of "KV cache"), and some proper nouns may be misrecognized.
